rejected.title: Nuremberg trials and the Genocide Convention
card: After World War II, the Allied powers put leading Nazis on trial in the German city of Nuremberg. The first trial began in November 1945.

The accused were charged with crimes such as war crimes and crimes against humanity. The trials held that leaders could be punished for what they did, even if they said they were only following orders.
Some of the accused were sentenced to death, some to prison, and some were found not guilty.

In 1948 the United Nations agreed the Genocide Convention. It made genocide, the deliberate destruction of a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, a crime that countries promised to prevent and punish.
rejected.remember: Nuremberg tried Nazi leaders for their crimes. The Genocide Convention aimed to prevent and punish genocide.

a.q: What did the Nuremberg trials show about leaders who commit war crimes?
opts: They could be tried and punished for their actions
They could not be tried once the war had ended
They were safe if they said they followed orders
They could only be judged by their own country
a.why: The trials put Nazi leaders in court and held them responsible for their crimes. Saying they were only following orders did not protect them, so the idea that orders are a defence is wrong.
a.clue: Think about what happened to the accused in the courtroom.

b.q: In 1948 a group of countries wants an agreement that makes the deliberate destruction of a religious group a crime. Which one fits?
opts: The Genocide Convention, agreed by the United Nations
The Nuremberg trials, which began in 1945
The Genocide Convention, agreed by the Allied generals
The Nuremberg trials, which began in 1948
b.why: The Genocide Convention was agreed by the United Nations in 1948 and made genocide a crime to prevent and punish. The Nuremberg trials were court cases against Nazi leaders that began in 1945, not an agreement between countries.
b.clue: One was a set of trials, the other was an agreement.

version.title: Nuremberg trials and the Genocide Convention
card: From November 1945, the Allies put leading Nazis on trial before an international court in the German city of Nuremberg.
They were charged with crimes such as war crimes and crimes against humanity, including the murder of civilians. The court ruled that following orders was no defence.
Twelve were sentenced to death, others went to prison, and three were found not guilty. The trials showed that leaders could be held to account under international law.

In 1948 the United Nations agreed the Genocide Convention. Genocide is acts meant to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part, and countries that join promise to prevent and punish it.
version.remember: After the war, leaders were held to account in court, and genocide became a crime that countries promised to stop.

a.q: A Nazi official on trial at Nuremberg says he was just following orders. How did the court treat this?
opts: It ruled that following orders was no defence
It ruled that he could not be tried at all
It freed him, as orders came from his leaders
It sent his case to be tried in a German court
a.why: The court ruled that following orders was no defence, so officials were held responsible for what they did. Freeing someone because the orders came from above would have let them escape blame.
a.clue: Did the court let orders excuse the crime?

b.q: Under the 1948 Genocide Convention, which of these acts is genocide?
opts: Killing people to destroy a religious group
Bombing an army base during a declared war
Arresting protesters who march against a law
Making a country pay for damage it caused
b.why: Genocide is acts meant to destroy a national, ethnic, racial or religious group, in whole or in part. Bombing an army base is an act of war, but it does not aim to destroy a group of people for who they are.
b.clue: Which act aims to destroy a group of people?
